Tensorlake npm release ran a credential-stealing worm

Target: Tensorlake · repo
Date: 2026-10-07
Target Kind: library
Language: JavaScript
Cause: compromised_account_credentials
Impact: credential_theft, remote_code_execution
Phase: source

Synopsis

The official tensorlake 0.5.144 npm release added a preinstall loader. Installing the SDK with lifecycle scripts enabled launched a worm that stole credentials and attempted further propagation.

Story

Developers installing a toolkit for running AI-generated code in isolated sandboxes received a credential-stealing worm before they ever created a sandbox. Tensorlake's npm release 0.5.144 arrived on October 8 with an installation hook that launched the malware on the installing machine. SafeDep and Socket independently flagged the release within minutes, tracing the danger to the SDK that developers used to manage Tensorlake environments.

SafeDep reconstructed a compromise of the project's source and release process. On October 7, a repository administrator account added two payload files and an installation hook through GitHub's web interface, then revised the changes and set the package version. The account subsequently started the project's normal npm publication workflow. Trusted publishing delivered the poisoned source through the legitimate pipeline; provenance attached to sibling packages documented that build without establishing that its contents were safe.

The retained source snapshot contains the preinstall command, lib/setup.mjs, and the large Math_Symbol.js payload. SafeDep found that the loader obtained Bun and avoided recognized CI environments, letting the publishing job proceed while leaving downstream installations exposed. Socket described collection of cloud credentials, package tokens, SSH material, and AI-tool configuration, together with remote execution and propagation capabilities. A token-monitoring component also made recovery hazardous: the researchers documented destructive behavior tied to invalidated credentials.

npm removed the malicious version, and Tensorlake's maintainers reverted the source changes and released 0.5.145, according to SafeDep. That stopped this version's normal distribution but did not account for machines where it had already executed. The exposure began with installing the management SDK, outside the isolated environments it was meant to control. Neither the package's routine download volume nor a successful release job measured how many developers actually ran the payload.
